left_vessel_tower.description: A continuous vertical column of 4 stacked ornate vessels/urns occupying the entire left margin of the folio from top to near the bottom. Each vessel is distinct in size and detail: the topmost is smallest and most compact; the second is the tallest with elaborate banding; the third is mid-sized; the bottommost is the widest with a broad footed base. All share a family resemblance in form — rounded body, narrow neck, pedestal base — and color scheme. The column acts as a permanent left-margin illustration blocking text from x<215 throughout the folio. The @Lc labels (f99v.1, 14, 25, 36) correspond one-to-one with each vessel from top to bottom.
left_vessel_tower.color: Primary body: deep red (vermilion/red lead pigment), consistent across all 4 vessels. Decorative bands and rims: teal-blue (verdigris or azurite-based pigment), forming alternating horizontal stripes and ring details. Top cap of uppermost vessel: bright blue (more intense than the bands — possibly a second blue pigment or thicker application). Bead/dot decorations on banding: cream-white. Interior of vessel openings: blue-teal wash visible from above. Pedestal bases: warm tan/cream ink. The red-and-teal combination is visually identical to the vessel towers on f88r and f82r — same pigment source likely.

upper_red_root_specimens.description: A horizontal row of approximately 6 plant root or tuber specimens displayed across the upper zone of the folio. Each specimen consists of a compact root-head or bulb with multiple long fibrous roots hanging downward, and small sprig-like stems projecting upward. They are arranged in a loose row, as if hung or displayed for examination. The two leftmost specimens are darkest; the central ones are medium-toned; the rightmost are slightly lighter. All share the same basic morphology — compact root head + hanging fibrous tendrils. The @Lf labels f99v.2–9 annotate these specimens (8 labels for 6 specimens suggests some specimens have multiple labels or the labels annotate parts).
upper_red_root_specimens.color: Root heads and bulb bodies: deep crimson-red to vermilion (same red family as the vessel pigment but less orange — more a carmine or red lead applied thinly). Root tendrils: warm reddish-brown to dark brown (thinner application of the same red pigment mixed with iron gall ink). The overall tone is a warm red-brown spectrum. Sprig tips: very faint greenish or unpainted (parchment color). Background: cream parchment. These are the most vividly red plant specimens in the analyzed corpus.

upper_center_green_leaf.description: A single large, rounded leaf or cap-shaped green structure at the top-center of the folio, positioned above and between the red root specimens. It has a smooth, slightly lobed outline. The green pigment is flat and solid. This isolated green element provides the only green color in the upper zone, creating a strong visual contrast with the surrounding red specimens.
upper_center_green_leaf.color: Medium flat green (same malachite-like botanical green seen throughout the Voynich balneological and botanical sections). No shading or tonal variation — purely flat wash. Outline in dark ink.

upper_right_vessel_form.description: At the top-right corner of the folio, a vessel or vase-like form — possibly a container or stylized flower calyx. It has a narrow base widening into a cupped or flared form at the top. The interior of the vessel is colored red. This element is visually analogous to the left vessel tower but much smaller and without the stacking.
upper_right_vessel_form.color: Exterior: cream/parchment with dark ink outline. Interior/fill: red (vermilion). The red interior makes it echo the left vessel tower's color language despite its different position and scale.

upper_dark_seed_drop.description: A single dark brown-black ovoid or teardrop-shaped element in the upper zone, positioned center-right. It appears to be an isolated seed, pod, or fruit — a compact solid mass approximately 20×30 pixels in the original. It sits in the text-label zone as a visual punctuation mark among the labels and plant specimens.
upper_dark_seed_drop.color: Deep dark brown-black (iron gall ink or dark brown pigment, solid application). No fill — purely ink. The darkest single element in the upper zone.

second_zone_pink_root_specimens.description: A second horizontal row of plant specimens at mid-folio, approximately 5 individual root/bulb forms. These are notably paler and softer in color than the upper red specimens — a pinkish-salmon tone rather than deep crimson. Each has the same general morphology: bulb or root head with hanging fibrous roots. One central specimen appears larger and more dramatically rendered with sweeping root tendrils. The @Lf labels f99v.15–20 and @Lc label f99v.14 annotate this zone.
second_zone_pink_root_specimens.color: Salmon-pink to light reddish-brown (a distinctly lighter application of the red pigment, possibly mixed with more white lead, or a thinner wash). The palette shift from the deep-red upper specimens to these lighter pink ones is deliberate — possibly distinguishing plant species or stages. Root tendrils: warm light brown. Background: cream parchment.

second_zone_black_star_flower.description: Embedded within the second specimen zone, a single flower or asterisk-like form rendered entirely in deep black ink. It has multiple pointed petals radiating from a center, creating a star or spiky flower appearance. This is the only purely black-filled illustration element on this folio (vs. the dark-ink outlines elsewhere). It sits between two of the pink root specimens.
second_zone_black_star_flower.color: Solid deep black (concentrated iron gall ink). No pigment wash — purely ink drawing. The stark black creates extreme contrast with the salmon-pink specimens flanking it. This is one of the more unusual illustration elements in the balneological/pharmaceutical Voynich sections.

third_zone_brown_bulb_specimens.description: A third horizontal row of plant specimens in the lower-middle zone of the folio, approximately 6 bulb or root specimens. These are intermediate in color between the upper crimson and the second-zone pink — a warm reddish-brown to tan. They include forms that appear to be: tulip-like bulbs with curling root tendrils, fan-shaped roots, and pendant forms. The specimens show more morphological variety than the upper zones. The rightmost specimen in this group has distinctive blue ribbon-like curling tendrils (see separate anchor). Labels f99v.26–31 and @Lc f99v.25 annotate this zone.
third_zone_brown_bulb_specimens.color: Warm medium brown to reddish-brown (raw umber range). Some specimens are lighter tan/beige; others are deeper reddish-brown closer to the second-zone pink. Root tendrils: darker brown ink. Background: cream parchment.

third_zone_right_blue_ribbon_plant.description: At the rightmost position of the third specimen zone, a distinctive plant form unlike any other on the folio. It features long, curling, ribbon-like tendrils rendered in blue-teal pigment — the same blue used for the vessel tower decorations. The ribbons curl and loop organically, resembling a marine organism or decorative vine. This is the only specimen in the third row rendered in blue rather than brown/red pigment.
third_zone_right_blue_ribbon_plant.color: Primary color: blue-teal (same verdigris or azurite blue as the vessel tower banding). The blue is applied as a wash over ink outlines. The ribbon forms are translucent and fluid-looking. The presence of this blue specimen among the otherwise brown-toned third row creates a strong visual anomaly — possibly indicating a different plant family or a deliberate scribal color-coding system.

lower_right_green_creature.description: In the lower-right quadrant of the folio, a large and visually dramatic amorphous green form — one of the most striking illustrations in the analyzed corpus. It resembles a large marine creature, anemone, or stylized exotic plant with multiple rounded lobes or tentacle-like extensions emerging from a central mass. The form is broad and organic, occupying a substantial portion of the lower-right folio area. It has no obvious botanical analog — possibly a sea creature (jellyfish, anemone), an exotic plant bud, or a fantastical illustration. The label f99v.44 (@Lf) 'koleearol' appears at its lower edge.
lower_right_green_creature.color: Deep rich green (the deepest, most saturated green on this folio — darker and more opaque than the flat botanical greens of f49v or f87r). The green has clear tonal variation: darker at edges/lobes, slightly lighter in the body center, suggesting shading or layered pigment application. This is the most three-dimensionally rendered green element in all analyzed folios. Outline: dark ink. No other pigment — pure green and ink.

bottom_blue_green_vine.description: At the very bottom of the folio, sweeping across the full width, a large flowing vine, root, or aquatic plant form. It consists of multiple thick curving stems that cross and loop, creating an organic lattice or wave. Small rounded leaf or bud forms are distributed along the stems. The form spans nearly the full folio width and rises from below the composition into the lower text zone. It is rendered in a distinctive blue-green (teal) that differs from both the vessel blue and the leaf green seen elsewhere.
bottom_blue_green_vine.color: Blue-green teal (a unique pigment mixture or the blue-teal verdigris applied more thinly over a green base — the resulting hue is distinctly aquamarine/teal, unlike any other element on this folio). Stem outlines: dark ink, visible beneath the wash. The teal color and aquatic/vine quality of this element strongly suggests it represents a water plant or marine organism rather than a terrestrial botanical specimen.

paragraph_zone_bisector_upper.description: The visual element causing the <-> bisections in paragraph block 1 (lines 10–13). Based on image analysis, this appears to be a plant stem or horizontal root element crossing the text band between the upper red specimens and second pink zone. A dark/brown stem or root form crosses horizontally at approximately y=240–350, splitting each paragraph line into left and right segments.
paragraph_zone_bisector_upper.color: Dark warm brown (same ink/pigment as root tendrils). The bisecting element is a natural extension of one of the upper plant specimens' root systems crossing into the text zone.

paragraph_zone_bisector_lower.description: The visual element causing the systematic <-> bisections in paragraph block 4 (lines 37–42). This is most likely the stem connecting the third-zone specimens to the lower right green creature — a long descending stem or the beginning of the lower_right_green_creature's body, positioned at approximately x=530–570 and running from y=760 down to y=850.
paragraph_zone_bisector_lower.color: Dark ink stem or the edge of the deep green lower creature. The bisection gap is narrower than those caused by the vessel tower, suggesting a thinner organic element.
